## Data

### Developmental History

Elliot Daniel Carter was born May 15, 2013 to his parents, Daniel and Rachel Morgan Carter. Elliot is an only child. Family relationships are reported as close and supportive. There is a family history of dyslexia, ADHD, anxiety, Bipolar Disorder, and depression.

Pregnancy with Elliot was reported with no complications. Elliot's birth was an emergency C-section when his mother started hemorrhaging and went into shock. Elliot was born weighing eight pounds, twelve ounces. He was described as a healthy baby with no resulting complications.

Early development was reported without significant delay. Walking, talking, and toileting were within normal limits. Elliot demonstrated good health and motor development as a child.

Elliot was taken to the emergency room on one occasion. When Elliot was three and a half (February 2017), he was assaulted by his day care provider resulting in a broken clavicle. Elliot was removed from the facility and legal action was taken. Following the incident, Elliot was aggressive at preschool. Elliot was evaluated by a doctor and it was determined his negative behavior was secondary to the abuse he received at day care. Elliot received individual therapy for three to four months to resolve anxiety and anger resulting from the abuse. His parents reported that therapy was very positive for Elliot.

Elliot is a healthy, physically active child. He demonstrates strong visual-spatial ability, according to his parents. At times, Elliot plays rough with other children. Elliot will not back down when bullied and can get into trouble when faced with another strong-willed child. The last few weeks of school, Elliot got into an incident with another child where the children were pushing each other back and forth. His parents stated that he is very compassionate with younger children.

Elliot's parents are concerned about pre-reading skills for Elliot. Elliot is learning his letters and working on writing his letters. At times, he will write words or letters backwards or will try to read letters up and down. Elliot tends to resist parent help by saying, "I know, I know." When things are challenging, Elliot will become frustrated and state, "I can't do that."

## Behavioral Observations

Elliot was tested and interviewed during two sessions (7/18/18, 8/21/18). He was appropriately dressed and oriented (X3) during the entire evaluation. Elliot demonstrated strong verbal expression skills. He did not appear tense and seemed comfortable with the examiner. Elliot was compliant with the examiner and seemed to want to do well. Elliot did demonstrate mild difficulty sitting still throughout the testing sessions. Breaks were taken during testing in order to sustain and increase attention. The examiner was present in the room during all testing including the Kiddie Conner's Continuous Performance Test (KCPT).

Elliot was administered ten scales from the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence-Forth Edition (WPPSI-IV). The WPPSI-IV is an individually administered, comprehensive clinical instrument for assessing the intelligence of children aged 2:6-7:7. The WPPSI-IVsubtest scores contribute to the index scores, which represent intellectual functioning in five cognitive areas: Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI), Visual Spatial Index (VSI), Fluid Reasoning Index (FRI), Working Memory Index (WMI), and the Processing Speed Index (PSI). This assessment also produces a Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) composite score. For the index scores and the FSIQ, scores ranging from 90 to 109 are considered average. The scores obtained on the WPPSI-IV reflect Elliot's true abilities combined with some degree of measurement error. Some children perform at approximately the same level in all of these areas, but most children display areas of cognitive strength and weaknesses.

The FSIQ is derived from six subtests and summarizes ability across a diverse set of cognitive functions. This score is typically considered the most representative indicator of general intellectual functioning. Elliot's FSIQ was in the Superior range when compared to other children his age (FSIQ = 120) and at the 91st percentile. While the FSIQ provides a broad representation of cognitive ability, describing Elliot's domain-specific performance allows for a more thorough understanding of his functioning in distinct areas.

The Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI) measured Elliot's ability to access and apply acquired word knowledge. Specifically, this score reflects his ability to verbalize meaningful concepts, think about verbal information, and express himself using words. Overall, Elliot's performance on the VCI was in the superior range (SS = 129) for his age and emerged as a relative strength for Elliot. High scores in this area indicate a well-developed verbal reasoning system with good word knowledge acquisition, effective information retrieval, a <!-- PageBreak --> strong ability to reason and solve verbal problems, and effective communication of knowledge. Elliot performed at the 97th percentile.

With regard to individual subtests within the VCI, Similarities required Elliot to describe a similarity between two words that represent a common object or concept and Information required him to recall rote memory of verbal information. He performed similarly on these two subtests suggesting that his verbal knowledge and his abstract verbal reasoning skills are similarly developed.

The Visual Spatial Index (VSI) measured Elliot's ability to evaluate visual details and understand visual spatial relationships in order to construct geometric designs from a model. This skill requires visual spatial reasoning, integration and synthesis of part-whole relationships, attentiveness to visual detail, and visual-motor integration. Elliot's performance was appropriate for his age (VSI = 100) and in the average range (50th percentile).

The VSI is derived from two subtests. During Block Design, Elliot viewed a model and/or picture and used two-colored blocks to recreate the design. The Object Assembly subtest required him to assemble the pieces of puzzles to create pictures of common objects. Elliot showed similar performance on these tasks. This pattern of scores suggests that his ability to analyze and synthesize abstract visual information is similar to his ability to understand part-whole relationships and engage in trial-and-error learning.

The Fluid Reasoning Index (FRI) measured Elliot's ability to detect the underlying conceptual relationship among visual objects and use reasoning to identify and apply rules. Identification and application of conceptual relationships in the FRI requires inductive and quantitative reasoning, broad visual intelligence, simultaneous processing, and abstract thinking. Overall, Elliot's performance was high average for his age (SS = 114, 82nd percentile).

The FRI is derived from two subtests: Matrix Reasoning and Picture Concepts. Matrix Reasoning required Elliot to select the missing pieces in incomplete patterns. On Picture Concepts, he was asked to choose pictures from two or three rows to form a group with a common trait. He performed comparably across both subtests, suggesting that his perceptual organization and categorical reasoning skills are similarly developed at this time.

The Working Memory Index (WMI) involves attention, concentration, and mental control. The WMI measures specific aspects of working memory such as visual working memory, visual-spatial working memory, and the ability to resist interference from previously memorized items. In the area of working memory, Elliot exhibited consistent performance on the WMI, and his overall performance was above that of other children his age (SS = 118, 88th percentile). Elliot's performance on working memory tasks was stronger than some cognitive abilities indicating an area of relative strength.

Within the WMI, The Picture Memory (PM) subtest required Elliot to memorize pictures and identify them on subsequent pages. On the Zoo Locations (ZL) subtest, he memorized the location of animal cards on a map and then placed the cards in the same location. He performed similarly across these two subtests.

The Processing Speed Index (PSI) measured Elliot's speed and accuracy of visual identification, decision making, and decision implementation. Performance on the PSI is related to visual scanning, visual discrimination, short-term memory, visuomotor coordination, and concentration. His overall processing speed was average for his age (SS = 100, 50th percentile).

<!-- PageBreak -->

The PSI is derived from two timed subtests. During the Bug Search (BS) subtest, he marked pictures of bugs in a search group that matched a target bug. The Cancellation (CA) subtest required him to mark target objects in a random and structured array.

The Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Achievement-Fourth Edition (WJ-IV), Form A, was used to assess Elliot's academic ability. Elliot, with a chronological age of 5 years, 2 months, achieved a Total Achievement score of 97 and placed in the average range for overall achievement. He placed in the 43rd percentile. Elliot's overall academic ability is lower than would be expected given his IQ which suggests possible academic weaknesses or diagnoses. Direct comparisons can be made among Elliot's achievement scores to help determine the presence and significance of any strengths and weaknesses among his abilities.

When compared to others at his age level, Elliot's academic skills (SS = 97, 43rd percentile) were in the average range and his ability to apply academic skills (SS = 102, 56th percentile) were in the average range. Of these areas of assessment, Elliot demonstrated strength for his ability to apply academic knowledge.

When compared to others at his age level, Elliot's Reading score is within the average range (SS = 97, 42'd percentile). Basic Reading Skills (SS = 93, 32'd percentile) were average. Demonstrated reading performance was in the average range. His Phoneme-Grapheme Knowledge was also in the average range (SS = 96, 39th percentile).

Elliot's Broad Mathematics score (SS = 110, 75th percentile) was in the high average range. His Math Calculation Skills (SS = 104, 60th percentile) scores was in the average range. He demonstrated stronger ability for math word problems (Applied Problems-superior range) than he did for paper pencil traditional math computations (Calculation-<!-- PageBreak -->high average range) and speeded (timed) simple computations (Math Fluency-low average range). For mathematic performance, having a test timed, did significantly impact performance compared to peers. It appeared that fine motor ability made rapid performance difficult for Elliot.

Written ability is an area of relative weakness for Elliot. Written Language (SS = 92, 39th percentile) was within the average range. Written language subtests were low average (Spelling) or average (Writing Samples). Fine motor skills appear to impact his ability to express himself in written form.

Even though the majority of Elliot's academic test scores fell within the average range, they are significantly lower than his cognitive ability suggesting an academic weakness or learning disorder. Two composite scores (Basic Reading Skills and Written Language) met criteria for a learning disorder. According to State of Washington Severe Discrepancy Tables, Elliot, with an overall IQ score of 120, would meet criteria for a learning disorder for academic composite areas scoring equal to or below 95 (criterion score). His performance on these two composite areas was below the criterion score and 27 points below demonstrated intellectual ability. Elliot's demonstrated hand writing did indicate some fine motor delays and his performance did show a weakness for written expression. Addressing this area of difficulty is recommended to strengthen overall academic performance.

## Adaptive Functioning

### VMI

To further examine the presence of fine motor skill difficulties, Elliot was administered the Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration (VMI) designed to assess perceptual organization and fine motor skills. Elliot was asked to copy simple shapes and images using pencil and paper. His performance indicated low average ability (83, 13th percentile, AE = 4-10). Elliot demonstrated an immature pencil grip, and his performance demonstrated significant delays compared to cognitive ability. This score indicates a possible developmental coordination disorder.

Elliot's father and mother completed the Gilliam Autism Rating Scale-Third Edition (GARS-3). This scale is designed to assess symptoms characteristic to Autism Spectrum Disorder (ADS), a pervasive developmental disorder characterized by markedly abnormal development in social interaction, communication, and restricted repertoire of activities and interests. The GARS-3 is used for the assessment of individuals ages 3 through 22 who present unique behavioral problems. The GARS-3 comprises six subscales and an overall <!-- PageBreak --> Autism Index (AI). The six subscales include: Restricted/Repetitive Behaviors, Social Interaction, Social Communication, Emotional Responses, Cognitive Style, and Maladaptive Speech.

When comparing Elliot's scores to a population of children with an Autism Spectrum Disorder diagnosis, Elliot's scores suggest that overall the probability of Elliot having ASD is Probable. Elliot had an Autism Index score of 69 (2nd percentile of individuals with ASD). His scores are ranked at severity level 1 (0 = not ASD, ASD scores are ranked 1, 2, 3 with 3 being the most severe). This level of severity indicates that symptoms are mild and may meet criteria for an Autism Spectrum Disorder.

Elliot's highest scores were the Emotional Responses and the Cognitive Style subscales. These scores were in the 25th and 75th percentiles of children with an Autism Spectrum Disorder. This level of emotional responses and cognitive rigidity is highly unusual and indicative of clinical levels of mood lability and poor mental flexibility. However, his overall score suggests a risk for ASD, but does not fully support this diagnosis given the low scores for Social Interaction and Social Communication.

The PKBS-2 contains five subscales assessing social development and problem behaviors: Social Cooperation, Social Interaction, Social Independence, Externalizing Problems, and Internalizing Problems. Higher Social Skills indicate greater levels of social adjustment. Higher Problem Behavior scores indicate greater levels of problem behavior.

Elliot's overall social scores indicate strong social awareness, good social communication, and appropriate social independence.

For the Problem Behavior Composite (higher scores indicate greater level of problem behavior), Elliot scored a standard score of 102 for his mother, but a 124 (elevated) for his father. Elliot's score of 130 from his father placed him in the range of High Risk while the score from his mother placed Elliot in the average range. Both parents indicated a tendency toward externalizing problems rather than internalizing problems. Elliot is more likely to act in inappropriate ways when experiencing intense emotions. While his scores were generally in the average range,

Elliot's scores suggest overall adequate social skills with no pervasive developmental disorder, but indicate possible clinical behavioral difficulty. Elliot's score indicate a risk for Oppositional Defiant Disorder.

Elliot completed the Kiddie Conners' Continuous Performance Test, a monotonous, computer test of attention. This task evaluates ability to sustain attention and inhibit impulsivity while performing a boring task. When compared to other children his age, Elliot's performance indicated that there is an equal chance that his profile comes from a group without attention problems or a group with attention problems. The confidence index of 50.0% means there is a 50.0% chance that this profile comes from a group without attention problems or a group with attention problems.

Various index scores within the KCPT, provide insight into Elliot's ability to attend. Scores are reported as T-scores (60-65 borderline clinical, >= 65 clinical). Elliot's performance demonstrated a mixed profile with some scales falling within the average range and some scales being clearly in the clinical range. While Elliot's performance suggests that he does not fully meet criteria for a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, he may demonstrate mild attention symptoms.

## Impressions

Daniel Elliot Carter is a five year old boy who is preparing to start kindergarten. He has a family history of dyslexia and his parents have observed early indicators of reading struggle. According to test results, his cognitive ability is within the superior range overall with significant strengths for verbal reasoning and working memory. Academic ability was in the high average range with a strength for math reasoning and a weakness for timed math paper-pencil calculation and spelling. Due to his age and developmental level, only one timed test was administered. The delayed performance for Math Fluency is likely due to slowed fine motor response time.

The question of Dyslexia or Specific Learning Disorder was raised due to a strong family history of reading difficulty. Elliot's history suggested a pattern of letter, word, and number reversals. According to State of Washington Severe Discrepancy Tables, Elliot, with an overall IQ score of 120, would meet criteria for a learning disorder for academic composite areas scoring equal to or below 95 (criterion score). His performance on Basic Reading Skills and Written Language was below the criterion score and 27 points below demonstrated intellectual ability. Elliot qualifies for a Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in reading and written expression.

Elliot's demonstrated hand writing on achievement testing did indicate fine motor delays. The VMI was administered to determine the level of fine motor delay. His performance on the VMI indicated a significant delay in fine motor ability. Because Elliot is still quite young and has not yet been exposed to a great deal of fine motor tasks, the diagnosis of a Developmental Coordination Disorder is withheld. If after first grade, Elliot continues to demonstrate significant delays in handwriting, he would meet criteria for this diagnosis.

Other areas of concern indicated during testing include attention span (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder), oppositional defiance (Oppositional Defiant Disorder), and social skills (Autism Spectrum Disorder). While some features were evidenced through test results, none of these three diagnoses demonstrated sufficient evidence to support a clinical diagnosis. Elliot demonstrated appropriate social skills, cooperation, and attention skills throughout testing. Results during testing were mixed suggesting that Elliot may at times demonstrate negative behaviors such as restlessness, poor peer cooperation, rigid thinking, and oppositional behavior. These areas should continue to be monitored and supported through positive parent-child interaction, good peer relationships, and age appropriate demands.

<!-- PageBreak -->

**Diagnosis:** Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in reading (F81.0), Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in written expression (F81.81), Rule-out Developmental Coordination Disorder

## Recommendations

1. It is recommended that Elliot' parents work closely with his teachers.
    - **a.** It is recommended that Elliot's parents meet with the school to establish an IEP to address reading, writing, and fine motor skills.
    - **b.** Regarding his reading ability, Elliot will benefit from support in this area. Support should come from the school but can also be addressed at home. Well-structured phonics-based programs tend to be the most effective interventions for young children, but parents, teachers, and tutors should utilize a combination of reading skill development strategies including phonics training, sight word recognition (whole-word teaching), and literature immersion. Continue multiple interventions in small group settings or one-on-one such as special education pull-out reading support, after school tutoring, parent reading, and self-reading (both in the presence of an adult and alone). Choose reading materials based on Elliot's areas of interest. Do some fun reading every day.

    - **c.** Written expression ability, including fine motor skill development as well as spelling and sentence construction, should be addressed explicitly. Using verbal statement, mental visualization, auditory experiencing, and written expression in combination when developing skills will help skill development and retention. Find ways to make these tasks fun, such as writing with his finger in a pan of flour, chalkboard writing, tracing an image of a superhero using tracing paper, or writing speech bubbles for a comic book.
    - **d.** Teachers can find ways to build self-confidence like touching a shoulder when behavior is appropriate or school work is accurate.

    - **e.** Time constraints should be removed from tests.
    - **f.** A home program to use after school hours or during the summer could be "Teach Your Child to Read in 100 Easy Lesson" by Siegried Engelmann, Phyllis Haddox, and Elaine Bruner. This program is intense and highly structured and provides parents with specific scripts regarding how to instruct.

    - **g.** To increase word recognition, Elliot's parents can begin by printing common names for household objects, laminating the words, and taping them around the house. Frequent exposure to words with the associated object will aid word recognition.

2. It is recommended that Elliot's parents continue to create a supportive home environment where Elliot can feel secure and successful.
    - **a.** To help prepare for the week and reduce transition difficulty, Elliot's parents can establish weekly family meetings to discuss past week's behavior and goals for the upcoming week with reinforcement established as motivators. Meetings should be short (about 20 minutes) and should <!-- PageBreak --> begin and end positively. Begin by talking about what went well during the week and end the meeting by having refreshments or playing a game. During the meeting, the family can review the calendar for the week and make plans for some family fun time. Early planning and awareness of events reduces anxiety and frustration that arises when events are unexpected or forgotten.
    - **b.** It is recommended that Elliot's parents set aside at least 30 minutes twice each week (one session with each parent) for one-on-one time with Elliot to facilitate emotional expression and foster positive relationships with others. Consistent one-on-one time with a child and parent is an effective intervention for fostering emotional stability and positive self-concepts in children. Positive self-concepts help children believe they have the ability to deal with negative emotions and feel understood and heard. Particularly when interactions are tense, coaching by a therapist in an office is generally an effective way to teach parents appropriate intervention skills and then transition the one-on-one times to the home. The goal of this time is to create a warm, safe environment, and so parents should set aside expectations that might make these activities tenser.

    - **c.** Refrain from corporal punishments such as spanking. While this type of intervention may appear to curb negative behavior in the short term, research suggests that it increases the likelihood of anxiety and aggressive behavior in children long-term.
    - **d.** Parents can help Elliot during times of stress by practicing with him and reminding his of relaxation techniques, verbalizing an understanding of his feelings, and conveying a message that they believe he has the ability to deal with the frustration.

    - **e.** Due to the parenting challenges that may arise with Elliot, it is recommended that his parents receive parent training from a mental health provider. Parent training will focus on avoiding power struggles, staying calm in the face of conflict, reinforcing positive behavior, establishing consistency in schedule and consequences, and fostering positive parent-child relationships and sense of family (family meetings, family time, family responsibilities).

3. Other interventions that are helpful with children include:
    - **a.** Using visual reminders such as charts of chores, detailed calendars of activities (use pictures if possible), reinforcement charts.
    - **b.** Keeping routines consistent, structured, and predictable as possible. When possible, prepare Elliot in advance for changes and transitions, including things such as schedule breaks, vacation days, etc.

    - **c.** When Elliot does not appear to listen - the act of 'singing' your words can have a beneficial effect.
    - **d.** Use turn taking activities as much as possible. Games that require turn taking are excellent ways to develop this skill.

    - **e.** Try to identify stress triggers - avoid them if possible -be ready to distract with some alternative 'come and see this ... ' etc. Preparation before leaving home or entering a store with a goal or focus for appropriate <!-- PageBreak --> behavior can give Elliot a distraction for the overstimulation inherent in social contexts.
    - **f.** Creativity is key. What might work today, may not tomorrow. Team work is exceptionally helpful in generating new ideas for intervention. Ideas like using touch screen computers to teach, puppets to communicate, and nature to sooth arise from trying to see the world from Elliot's perspective and attempting to enter his world in a way that helps his connect with ours.
